_readme: Curated, hand-picked list for the 'Case Files' series — deliberately NOT auto-generated by AI, to keep this content type limited to only extremely well-documented, legally-resolved-or-non-accusatory financial cases. Edit this file freely: remove anything you're not comfortable covering, add new ones (same shape), or reorder priority. facts_brief entries are Claude's general-knowledge summary of well-known public facts, NOT independently source-verified via live research this session — treat them as a starting anchor, not a final source. Videos default to PRIVATE upload; review each one for accuracy before flipping public.

topics.subject: Bernie Madoff's Ponzi Scheme
topics.facts_brief: Bernard Madoff ran the largest Ponzi scheme in history through his investment firm, paying returns to earlier investors using money from new investors rather than real profits. It collapsed in December 2008 amid the financial crisis when redemption requests exceeded new investment. He confessed to his sons, who reported him to the FBI; he was arrested December 11, 2008. He pleaded guilty in March 2009 to 11 felony counts and was sentenced to 150 years in prison. Investor losses were estimated around $65 billion in paper wealth (roughly $17-20 billion in actual principal invested). He died in prison in April 2021.

topics.subject: Enron's Collapse
topics.facts_brief: Enron, once the 7th-largest company in the US, collapsed in December 2001 after it emerged executives had used off-balance-sheet special purpose entities (notably ones tied to CFO Andrew Fastow) to hide billions in debt and inflate profits. The company filed for bankruptcy in December 2001, then the largest bankruptcy in US history. Auditor Arthur Andersen was convicted of obstruction of justice (later overturned) and collapsed as a firm. CEO Jeffrey Skilling was convicted on multiple fraud counts (sentence later reduced); founder Kenneth Lay was convicted but died before sentencing; Fastow pleaded guilty and cooperated with prosecutors. Roughly 20,000 employees lost jobs and retirement savings tied up in company stock.

topics.subject: WorldCom's Accounting Fraud
topics.facts_brief: WorldCom, a major telecom company, collapsed in 2002 after disclosing it had improperly classified roughly $3.8 billion (later found to be over $11 billion) in operating expenses as capital expenditures, inflating profits. It was the largest accounting fraud and bankruptcy (at the time) in US history. CEO Bernard Ebbers was convicted of fraud and conspiracy in 2005 and sentenced to 25 years; CFO Scott Sullivan pleaded guilty and cooperated. Roughly 30,000 employees were laid off.

topics.subject: Lehman Brothers' 2008 Collapse
topics.facts_brief: Lehman Brothers, a 158-year-old investment bank, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 — the largest bankruptcy filing in US history (~$639 billion in assets) — after heavy exposure to subprime mortgage-backed securities and failed efforts to find a buyer or government bailout. Its collapse is widely regarded as the pivotal moment that accelerated the 2008 global financial crisis. A court-appointed examiner's report (the Valukas Report) detailed aggressive accounting practices ("Repo 105") used to temporarily move debt off the balance sheet before reporting periods. No Lehman executives were criminally charged.

topics.subject: Theranos and Elizabeth Holmes
topics.facts_brief: Theranos, founded by Elizabeth Holmes, claimed to have developed technology that could run hundreds of medical tests from a few drops of blood. Investigative reporting (notably by John Carreyrou at the Wall Street Journal starting 2015) revealed the technology didn't work as claimed and the company was secretly using traditional lab equipment. The company, once valued at $9 billion, dissolved in 2018. Holmes and former COO/president Ramesh 'Sunny' Balwani were charged with fraud; Holmes was convicted in January 2022 on four counts of investor fraud and sentenced to over 11 years; Balwani was also convicted and sentenced.

topics.subject: FTX's Collapse and Sam Bankman-Fried
topics.facts_brief: FTX, a major cryptocurrency exchange founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, collapsed in November 2022 after reporting revealed it had improperly used customer funds via its affiliated trading firm Alameda Research to cover losses and fund risky bets, rather than keeping customer deposits segregated. It filed for bankruptcy November 11, 2022. Bankman-Fried was arrested and, in November 2023, convicted on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy; he was sentenced in March 2024 to 25 years in prison. Estimated customer/investor losses were in the billions of dollars, though bankruptcy recovery efforts later recovered a large portion of funds.

topics.subject: Long-Term Capital Management's 1998 Collapse
topics.facts_brief: Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) was a hedge fund founded in 1994 by, among others, John Meriwether, with two Nobel laureate economists (Myron Scholes and Robert Merton) on its board, using highly leveraged trading strategies. In 1998, following Russia's debt default, LTCM's positions moved sharply against it, and with leverage reportedly exceeding 25-to-1, the fund faced catastrophic losses in weeks. Fearing a systemic risk to the broader financial system, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York organized a $3.6 billion bailout by a consortium of banks (no direct taxpayer funds) in September 1998. No fraud was alleged — this is a case study in leverage and risk management, not wrongdoing.

topics.subject: WeWork's Failed IPO and Adam Neumann
topics.facts_brief: WeWork, a shared office-space company co-founded by Adam Neumann, was privately valued at around $47 billion before attempting to go public in 2019. Its IPO filing (S-1) revealed massive losses, unconventional corporate governance (including Neumann holding outsized voting control and various related-party transactions, such as WeWork leasing buildings Neumann personally owned), and questions about its business model. The IPO was withdrawn in September 2019, Neumann was ousted as CEO with a large exit package funded by major investor SoftBank, and the company's valuation collapsed. WeWork eventually went public via SPAC in 2021 at a fraction of its earlier valuation and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023. No criminal fraud charges were involved — primarily a governance and valuation case study.

topics.subject: Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 Collapse
topics.facts_brief: Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), a major lender to tech startups and VC firms, failed on March 10, 2023, in the second-largest bank failure in US history at the time. SVB had invested a large share of deposits in long-dated Treasury and mortgage-backed securities; as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates through 2022-23, those securities lost significant market value. When depositors (many with balances over the FDIC's $250,000 insurance limit) began withdrawing amid concern, it triggered a rapid bank run (helped along by social media/group chats among VCs), and regulators closed the bank within about 48 hours. The FDIC and Treasury took the unusual step of guaranteeing all deposits, even above the insured limit, to prevent wider contagion. This is primarily an interest-rate-risk and bank-run case study, not a fraud case.

topics.subject: MF Global's Collapse and Jon Corzine
topics.facts_brief: MF Global, a commodities brokerage led by former Goldman Sachs CEO and NJ Governor/Senator Jon Corzine, collapsed into bankruptcy in October 2011 after risky bets on European sovereign debt. In the chaotic final days, roughly $1.6 billion in customer segregated funds went missing (later mostly recovered) as the firm scrambled to cover a liquidity crunch — segregated customer funds are legally required to be kept separate from firm money. It was the 8th-largest bankruptcy in US history at the time. Corzine faced a civil enforcement action from the CFTC and agreed in 2017 to pay a $5 million personal penalty and a lifetime ban from the futures industry; he was not criminally charged.
